title: Chandipura Virus Kills 10 Children in Gujarat as Monsoon Outbreak Widens
excerpt: Gujarat has confirmed 26 cases and 150 suspected infections of the sandfly-borne virus that causes fatal brain inflammation in children, with Rajasthan also reporting cross-border cases.
body:
• Gujarat has confirmed 26 Chandipura virus cases and 10 deaths this monsoon season, with 150 suspected cases under investigation across the state
  • The sandfly-borne virus primarily affects children under 15, causing acute encephalitis that can turn fatal within 24 hours of symptom onset
  • Rajasthan has also reported cases, with three patients from the state dying in Gujarat hospitals, prompting cross-border surveillance efforts
  • No vaccine or specific treatment exists for the virus; health authorities have trained nearly 2,000 pediatricians and deployed rapid response teams across affected districts

Gujarat's monsoon season has brought a familiar public health crisis back to its doorstep. The Chandipura virus, a sandfly-borne pathogen that causes deadly brain inflammation in children, has killed at least 10 people and infected 26 others across the state since June, according to data from the Gujarat health department.

The outbreak, centered in the state's rural heartland, has prompted authorities to place the health machinery on high alert. A total of 150 suspected cases have been reported statewide, with samples undergoing analysis at the Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre in Gandhinagar.

A Rapid and Lethal Pathogen

Chandipura virus belongs to the Rhabdoviridae family and was first identified in India in 1965 in a village near Nagpur, Maharashtra. It spreads primarily through the bite of infected sandflies, though some studies suggest mosquitoes and ticks may also serve as vectors. The virus is not contagious between humans.

What makes it particularly dangerous is its speed. Symptoms — sudden high fever, vomiting, seizures, and loss of consciousness — can escalate to full-blown acute encephalitis syndrome within 24 hours, according to health officials. Children under 15 are disproportionately affected, and the case fatality rate in confirmed infections remains alarmingly high.

"If any child develops symptoms such as sudden high fever, seizures, vomiting, diarrhoea or unconsciousness, parents should immediately contact the nearest government hospital or a paediatric specialist without wasting any time."

— Praful Pansheriya, Gujarat Health Minister

Outbreak Spreads Across Districts

The confirmed cases have been reported across multiple districts, including Panchmahal, Kheda, Sabarkantha, Mehsana, Bharuch, Bhavnagar, and areas under the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation. Three of the 10 confirmed deaths involved children from neighboring Rajasthan who had traveled to Gujarat for treatment.

Neelam Patel, Additional Director of Gujarat's Health Department, confirmed that of the 26 positive cases, three patients have recovered and been discharged. However, nine test results remain pending, leaving the final toll uncertain.

The outbreak has also triggered alarm in Rajasthan, which has reported four confirmed cases and at least two deaths linked to the virus. Rajasthan's health department has launched door-to-door surveys and health camps in Dungarpur, Sirohi, and Udaipur districts.

Government Response and Diaspora Concern

Gujarat has mobilized its public health infrastructure in response. Health Minister Pansheriya has chaired multiple review meetings, directing officials to investigate the travel and case histories of infected patients to trace transmission sources. Dusting and insecticide spraying operations are underway around mud houses and cattle sheds — the preferred habitats of sandflies — across affected areas.

The Indian Medical Association has issued guidelines to pediatric specialists statewide, and 1,993 pediatricians have received training through continuing medical education programs. Pediatric ICU beds, ventilators, and essential medicines have been made available at district hospitals across Gujarat.

For the Indian diaspora, the outbreak carries echoes of the devastating 2024 season, when Gujarat reported 38 confirmed Chandipura deaths with a speculative toll of 48. Families with young children planning monsoon visits to Gujarat and western Rajasthan are being advised to take precautions against sandfly bites, including wearing full-sleeved clothing and using mosquito nets.

What's Next

With the monsoon season expected to continue through September, health officials warn that cases may rise further. The virus is historically most active during this period due to heightened sandfly breeding. Gujarat has preemptively launched preventive measures at all 61 locations where cases were reported during the 2024 outbreak.

The absence of a vaccine or targeted antiviral treatment means prevention remains the primary defense. Authorities continue to urge parents across western and central India to seek immediate medical attention at the first sign of fever, seizures, or altered consciousness in children.
